title: Axar Patel Holds Nerve as India Survive Japan Scare in Historic Two-Run T20I Win
excerpt: Rain reduced the historic one-off T20I in Sano to five overs a side, and 41st-ranked Japan came within two runs of stunning the T20 world champions before Axar Patel held his nerve in the final over.
body:
• India survived an almighty scare in the historic one-off T20I at Sano, beating 41st-ranked Japan by two runs after rain reduced the match to five overs a side.
  • Japan's spinners stunned the T20 world champions, restricting India to 32 for 4 — with only captain Shreyas Iyer (16) reaching double figures — before Axar Patel defended eight runs in the final over.
  • A contentious wide call against a reverse-sweeping batter was overturned in the final over after Shreyas Iyer and Sanju Samson objected; with four needed off the last ball, Japan managed only one.
  • The win was India's 200th in T20 internationals — a first for any team — but Japan left with the moral victory after pushing the world's best side to the final delivery.

SANO, Japan — India escaped with a two-run victory over Japan in the historic one-off T20I at the Sano International Cricket Ground on Tuesday, surviving a final-ball thriller that the 41st-ranked hosts had no business being part of. After a delay of nearly three hours for a wet outfield reduced the contest to five overs per side, Japan's spinners humbled the reigning T20 world champions — and then came within a single boundary of beating them.

A batting collapse in five overs

Winning the toss, India captain Shreyas Iyer chose to bat on a slow wicket with a sluggish outfield. What followed was extraordinary. Abhishek Sharma was bowled for a golden duck in the first over by Brisbane grade cricketer Charlie Hara-Hinze, and Japan struck in each of the next two overs as well. Sanju Samson made 9 off 7, Ishan Kishan fell for 3, and only Iyer — 16 off 12 balls — reached double figures. Tilak Varma was left stranded on 1 not out as India crawled to 32 for 4, with Hara-Hinze (2 for 17), Ibrahim Takahashi (1 for 13) and Benjamin Ito-Davis sharing the wickets.

India's plan to lean on an all-spin attack looked like the right call when Japan slipped to 7 for 2 — Lachlan Yamamoto-Lake run out by a sharp Ishan Kishan throw, Takahashi dismissed by Washington Sundar. But captain Kendel Kadowaki-Fleming, who also plays grade cricket in Brisbane, kept Japan in the contest, and with Benjamin Ito-Davis the hosts reached 25 for 3 after four overs. Eight runs were needed off Axar Patel's final over.

Drama in the final over

What followed will be replayed for years in Japanese cricket circles. A delivery from Axar to the reverse-sweeping Alex Shirai-Patmore was initially called wide — then overturned after Iyer and wicketkeeper Samson argued that the batter's shot attempt made it a legitimate ball. Sundar had already struck on the final ball of the previous over to remove Kadowaki-Fleming for 12, and Axar held his nerve to the end: with four needed off the last ball, Shirai-Patmore could only manage a single. Japan finished on 30 for 3. Sundar, with two wickets, was India's best bowler.

"I'm extremely proud. When it gets that close, it's tougher to take. Emotions were running high and the fact we were able to run the best team in the world to the last ball is pretty special."

— Kendel Kadowaki-Fleming, Japan captain

Context: a milestone wrapped in a warning

The result marked India's 200th win in T20 internationals including Super Over victories — the first team to reach the landmark — and only the fourth time India have won a T20I by the two-run margin, after Sri Lanka in 2023, South Africa in 2012 and Bangladesh in 2016. But the numbers that will linger are Japan's: a side ranked 41st in the world, playing its first-ever T20I against India, restricting the world champions to 32 for 4 and taking the chase to the final ball in front of a healthy home crowd.

For the large Indian diaspora that follows the team everywhere, the match was also a glimpse of cricket's quiet globalisation: Japanese cricket's rise has been built in part on players of Indian origin, and match coverage noted the absence from the XI of Indian-origin players Abhishek Anand and Sabaorish Ravichandran. The sport's newest frontiers are increasingly being staffed by the diaspora itself.

What comes next

India will bank the win and the milestone, but the coaching staff will have questions about a batting display that bordered on shambolic against an attack few in the squad had faced before. For Japan, the narrow defeat is the kind of result that accelerates a cricketing culture — proof, delivered against the best team in the world, that the gap is closable. The two sides are unlikely to meet often, which only adds to the legend this five-over shootout will acquire in Sano.
image_caption: India captain Shreyas Iyer (right) shakes hands with Japan captain Kendel Kadowaki-Fleming at the pre-match press conference in Sano. India went on to edge Japan by two runs in the rain-reduced one-off T20I, with the 41st-ranked hosts pushing the world champions to the final ball.
nri_angle: Japan's cricketing rise is powered in part by players of Indian origin, making this historic first meeting between the sides a milestone for the diaspora's role in growing the game globally.
